notes.title: Applied Materials guided to a record. It needed an extra week to get there.
body: Thursday night, Applied Materials strutted out of earnings with a record in one hand and a forecast in the other. Friday morning, the paparazzi caught it slipping. By late morning the stock was near $365, down about 4%. Before anyone calls it a breakup, look around the room. SOXX, a fund that holds a basket of chip stocks, was down about the same. The session isn't over, so that's a snapshot, not a receipt.

Quick intro for the new kids. Applied doesn't make chips. It makes the machines that make chips: the tools that lay down, carve and polish the layers on a silicon wafer. Last quarter, revenue was $10.41 billion, up 53% from a year ago. The fiscal year came in at $34.45 billion. Everyone building AI factories needs these machines, and Applied is the one selling them.

Plot twist. Then came the guide, meaning management's forecast for next quarter: $11.1 billion, give or take $500 million. A record. Except on the call, the finance chief said it's a 14-week quarter. The one that just ended had 13. Split it per week and the new guide lands about 1% below what Applied just did. That's my math, not theirs. It's like bragging about your biggest Spotify Wrapped ever in a leap year. Technically true. You also had an extra day.

So is the glow-up fake? My read: no. On the call, the finance chief said clean room capacity “remains a gating factor,” and that “our Q1 number would be slightly higher if everything were perfectly available.” A clean room is the dust-free building where these machines get installed. Translation: customers want more tools than there are rooms to plug them into. And they're paying early. Contract liabilities, money customers paid before getting everything they ordered, hit $3.59 billion, up from $2.57 billion a year ago. Inventory climbed to $6.89 billion. That looks like a company stocking up to ship, not one waiting by the phone.

Here's who has the leverage. When buyers prepay and the bottleneck is buildings, the toolmaker isn't the one begging. CEO Gary Dickerson said the company's current view is that demand for chipmaking equipment rises more than 30% next year. Applied also spent $2 billion buying back its own stock last quarter. Looks like management likes the order book enough to bet its own cash on it.

One side-eye. China was 25% of revenue last quarter, down from 29% a year earlier, and the finance chief said shipments there will probably be under 25% of the business in 2027. Losing share with your biggest out-of-town customer is fine while everyone else is lining up. It's less fine if that line gets shorter.

I get the itch. A record quarter, a red morning, and your thumb is hovering over the buy button like it just got a restock alert. The catch: on Thursday the stock already slid 3.58% into the report while SOXX barely moved, so some of the doubt was priced in before anyone read a word. Buying this dip is a bet that the extra week is calendar noise, not makeup over slowing demand.

One thing on my calendar: Applied's February guide, for a normal 13-week quarter. If it's $11.1 billion or higher, this week's wobble was a calendar hiccup. If it comes in below that, the extra week was doing the heavy lifting, and my read was wrong.

So there's no pre-print positioning here to cash in or panic over. I'm watching whether today's red morning pulls fresh bets in or the crowd just shrugs.

notes.title: Nebius cashed a one-time bonus. Then it retired the scoreboard.
body: Wednesday, Nebius strutted into earnings like it already knew the verdict. The stock closed up 15.44%, at $154.69, the day after CoreWeave reported. SOXX, a fund that holds a basket of chip stocks, rose 6.01%. Then Thursday morning the report landed, and by late morning the stock was trading near $130. The session isn't over, so that's a snapshot, not a receipt.

Quick intro for the new kids. Nebius rents out AI computers. It fills data centers with Nvidia chips and leases the horsepower to people building AI. Third-quarter revenue was $980.8 million, up 571% from a year ago and up 68% from the second quarter. On the red carpet, that's a full glow-up.

Plot twist. In its shareholder letter, Nebius says about $325 million of that was non-recurring revenue, tied to what it calls its asset-light model. One-time money. Take it out and the quarter is roughly $656 million. Against $582.3 million in the second quarter, that's growth of about 13%. Still growth. Just not the 68% on the poster.

Same letter, one more line: “We no longer see ARR as the right measure of our business.” ARR means annual recurring revenue, the yearly pace of repeat sales, and it was the number this crowd lived by. It's like landing a one-time bonus, letting everyone think it's your salary, then announcing salary isn't a useful number anymore. Maybe there's a good reason. The timing is still the gossip. Nebius also now expects 2026 revenue at the low end of its $3.0 to $3.4 billion range.

Now the cash. Operating cash flow, the money the business actually brought in, was negative $273 million. Last quarter it was positive $2.25 billion. By the end of September, customers owed Nebius about $4.04 billion. My read: big prepaid deals got billed, but the checks hadn't cleared yet. Meanwhile it spent $7.3 billion on equipment in three months.

Here's the part I'll defend. The letter says prepayments on deals signed in the third quarter covered more than 100% of the related equipment spending. For 2027, it guides revenue of $12 to $13 billion and capital spending of $40 to $45 billion, with 75% to 85% of that covered by customer prepayments and loans backed by the gear. Pre-tax breakeven is pegged for the fourth quarter of 2027. So the customers are also the bank. That's leverage. It's also concentration: if a big tenant pays late, the landlord feels it fast.

I get the itch. A hot stock gives back a chunk in one morning, and your thumb starts calling it a markdown. The catch: buying here is a bet that those invoices turn into cash on schedule. If next quarter's operating cash flow is still negative, that bet is wrong.

One thing on my calendar: the next quarterly report. I want operating cash flow back above zero and that receivables pile shrinking. A bonus is nice. A paycheck that shows up every month is the business.

notes.flowRemark: The options bets I can see were placed Wednesday, before the letter, and the crowd leaned both ways: some bought protection months out, others bought calls that expire this week. The short-dated calls met a gap down. I'm watching whether the longer-dated insurance gets cashed in or rolled.

notes.title: CoreWeave sold out the tour. The fans are paying for the stage.
body: Tuesday night, CoreWeave walked into earnings looking like it slept in its car. The stock had dropped 9.32% in five sessions, to $48.73. SOXX, a fund that holds a basket of chip stocks, fell 5.43% over the same stretch. CNBC put the one-month slide near 40%. Then the numbers hit, and Wednesday morning it opened near $56. The session isn’t over, so that’s a snapshot, not a receipt.

Quick intro for the new kids. CoreWeave rents out AI computers. It fills data centers with Nvidia chips and leases the horsepower to AI labs. Last quarter, revenue was $3.661 billion, up 168% from a year ago. It raised its full-year sales target to $13.0 to $13.3 billion. And the backlog, meaning signed contracts it hasn’t delivered yet, hit about $132.5 billion. That’s a tour sold out for years.

Plot twist. The sold-out tour still lost money. The business earned $207 million in operating income, which is profit before interest and taxes. Interest on its debt cost $846 million. That’s four times what the show cleared at the door. Net loss: $709 million. The band is packing arenas, and the loan on the tour bus is eating the merch table.

And the loans are getting pricey. CNBC reported that some CoreWeave bonds recently yielded more than 16%, and that the finance chief told analysts the company doesn’t plan to sell more of that kind of debt through 2027 at those rates. So who pays for the next stage? CEO Michael Intrator said it in the release: “approximately $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits expected in the next three months alone.” Read that again. The fans are fronting the cash for the venue.

My read: that’s the real headline. When lenders want 16% and customers hand over deposits instead, the customers need the computers more than CoreWeave needs the bond market. That’s leverage, the good kind. It also means the same AI labs are now the tenant and the bank. If one of them slows down, both doors close at once.

I get the itch. A beaten-up stock jumps on a record quarter and your thumb starts doing math. The catch: capital spending, the money going into chips and buildings, is guided to $37 to $39 billion this year. That’s nearly three times the sales target. The company also told us interest runs $1.05 to $1.15 billion next quarter. Chasing the pop is a bet that the deposits keep showing up faster than the bills. If the prepayments come in light, that bet is wrong.

One thing on my calendar: the next quarterly report. I want to see that $9 billion actually land on the balance sheet. A sold-out tour is a promise. A deposit is a receipt. I’ll clap for the encore when the check clears.

notes.flowRemark: The options bets I can see were placed Tuesday, before the numbers dropped, and some of it looked like people buying short-dated protection going into the print. That insurance met a jump at the open. I’m watching whether the hedgers reload after the pop or quietly walk away.

notes.title: Google built its own lock. Then it called AMD.
body: Monday, the chip crowd limped back from a brutal week. AMD walked in with a fresh haircut and a story to tell. The stock closed up 13.26%, at $508.58. SOXX, a fund that holds a basket of chip stocks, rose 7.49%. Same session, nearly double the group’s bounce.

The story landed before the opening bell. AMD said its fifth-generation EPYC processors run the host side of Google Cloud’s new TPU 8tx. A TPU is Google’s own AI chip. The host CPU is the stage manager: it schedules the work, preps the data and keeps the TPUs fed. Google Cloud’s Mark Lohmeyer said the pairing brings hardware-enforced confidential computing to Cloud TPUs for the first time. In normal words, the data stays locked even while the machine is working on it. Model weights, prompts, the whole diary.

Plot twist. Google already makes its own server CPU. It’s called Axion, it’s Arm-based, and Google has run it alongside its recent TPUs so it leans less on outside chip vendors. So this is the homeowner who designed a custom lock, then handed the neighbor the spare key to the safe room. My read: when the job was security, Google decided the neighbor’s deadbolt was better. That’s a real compliment from a company that would love to need nobody.

Now rewind to Thursday. AMD fell 17.26% in one session, to $404.40, when the market dumped anything tied to AI data centers. Two sessions later, it closed 4.05% above Wednesday’s close. SOXX is still 2.25% under it. The rest of the class is icing its ankles. AMD is already running laps. Oppenheimer also upgraded the stock Monday, per Yahoo Finance’s recap, so the press release showed up with a hype man.

Here are the receipts I don’t have. Neither company put a dollar figure on this. No chip count. No price. No date for general availability, which is when any customer can actually rent the thing. This is a seating chart, not an invoice. A 13% day is a lot of applause for an announcement that hasn’t billed anyone yet.

I get the itch. The stock took a punch, got up swinging, and your thumb wants in like it’s a limited drop. The catch: buying after a 13% day means paying Monday’s price for news that may not show up in revenue for a while. And if Google’s next TPU quietly ships with Axion as the host, the chosen-one story gets a lot shorter. That’s what would prove the hype wrong.

One thing on my calendar: the day Google posts TPU 8tx pricing and a general-availability date. That’s when a press release turns into a bill. Until then, AMD has the spare key. I want to see who actually moves in.

notes.title: Nvidia ghosted the rally. The board has questions.
body: Monday’s market showed up to the party in sequins. Nvidia showed up in sunglasses, parked itself by the snack table and refused to dance. The index went green. The chip king went red. When the most popular kid skips the group photo, people start texting.

Here’s what we actually know. On Sunday, Nvidia’s board said it opened an independent investigation after reports that CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. Same statement, same breath: the board has no reason to think company secrets or national security were compromised. That’s corporate for “we’re checking the locks, nothing looks missing, please stop ringing the doorbell.” Cute. I’ll stop ringing when I see what the locksmith finds.

Also, this was not Nvidia’s first bad night out this week. Stocks partied after the midterms. Then Thursday flipped the lights on at 2 a.m. The Nasdaq fell 5.5%. SOXX, a fund that holds a basket of chip stocks, fell 12.15%. The worry: after Democrats won, new data centers could catch more fights over permits and power bills. That’s a fear about future fights, not a new law. But a GPU can write your wedding toast in nine languages and still can’t get the zoning board to text back. No building, no rack. No rack, no delivery.

Plot twist the timeline missed: Nvidia actually held up better than its friends. Five sessions through Nov. 6, Nvidia fell 8.8%. The chip fund fell 13.13%. Not a trophy. Still a receipt. Thursday was the whole squad getting dragged out of the club together. Monday was Nvidia doing the walk of shame alone while everyone else went to brunch. That’s when the board story earns its own headline. The chart shows me the split. It can’t tell me how much is scandal and how much is leftover hangover.

Now, the dip. I see you. It’s down, it’s Nvidia, and your thumb is hovering over buy like it’s hovering over an ex’s new story at 1 a.m. Very human. Also how people end up apologizing over coffee. Before I touch it, I want one receipt. Customers pushing deliveries? Show me dates. Shipping on time but getting paid slower? Show me the cash. Other chip names sliding again? Then it’s a group-chat problem, not an Nvidia scandal.

Because there’s a canyon between a customer saying “take the chips in March instead” and an investor whispering “what if they take the chips in March instead?” One moves real revenue out of the quarter. The other just moves the stock, before a single order changes. If someone swears a delay is real, ask for the project name and the date. Rumors never bring those. Receipts always do.

Nvidia reports Nov. 17, and I’ll be in the front row. Two questions. What did the board find? And did any customer actually move a delivery date? Until then, the chart gets one browser tab and the receipts get another. Yes, I have too many tabs. These two pay rent.
